content: Efforts were undertaken to enhance the process of preventing surgical site infections (SSIs) and to improve outcome measures. Activities and actions were consistently implemented across various sites, with additional local adaptations and initiatives described in the published article and its associated online appendix. Several tools provided by the Comprehensive Unit-based Safety Program (CUSP) and the World Health Organization (WHO) were adapted and utilized at the local level to support these efforts. Hospitals or surgical departments aiming to initiate a Surgical Unit-based Safety Program (SUSP) project must meet specific prerequisites. These include committing to an intensive 24-month implementation period while ensuring long-term sustainability and integration into routine practices. A multidisciplinary team must be assembled, including representatives from infection prevention and control (IPC), anesthesiology, and surgery units. Senior-level executives must be engaged as part of the team. Actions to improve perioperative teamwork, communication, and safety culture must be implemented. Regular team meetings should be held to monitor performance and implement interventions. Additionally, a minimal set of standardized surgical outcome data must be submitted monthly. Key aspects of the SUSP Africa intervention included leadership by local core teams, each involving at least one senior local surgeon. External experts provided training and mentorship on project management and data collection, primarily through webinars and monthly calls, with each site receiving one in-person visit lasting 3–4 days. Three inter-country meetings were held during the project, starting from the preparation phase. A small budget was allocated to each hospital, with restrictions on its use for equipment procurement, project-related products, or salaries, except for costs associated with research and data collection. A significant success of the intervention was its gradual integration into routine clinical practice. Local production or procurement of specific products became part of the regular budget. Hospital staff were highly motivated to improve their practices, and local project leaders were influential members of their respective departments. Key lessons learned from the SUSP Africa initiative emphasized the importance of using multimodal strategies for SSI prevention, rather than relying solely on checklists and bundles. A stepwise action plan for improvement interventions is essential. Prevention recommendations should be mapped according to the surgical patient journey to engage all levels of the local team. Empowering teams and involving frontline staff is critical, as is engaging leadership from the outset. Teams should take the lead in adapting interventions, fostering collective and individual ownership. Data should be used to create awareness, and teams should be recognized and rewarded while working within a safety culture framework. Resource investment, including assessment, observation, monitoring, and learning from defects, must be acknowledged and embedded into local workflows. The WHO multimodal approach for SSI prevention is based on evidence and global experience, demonstrating that behavioral change and healthcare-associated infection (HAI) reduction are achievable through integrated improvement strategies. This approach involves five key components: system change, training and education, monitoring and feedback, reminders and communications for awareness-raising, and fostering a safety climate and culture change. Each component is essential for translating guideline recommendations into practice, engaging all stakeholders, and ensuring actions are relevant to the local setting. System change involves ensuring the necessary infrastructure and resources are in place to facilitate SSI prevention. Training and education focus on equipping healthcare workers with practical knowledge of evidence-based SSI prevention practices. Monitoring and feedback involve regular evaluation of practices, infrastructure, and outcomes, coupled with timely feedback to identify areas for improvement. Reminders and communications serve to reinforce the importance of SSI prevention practices and inform patients and staff about expected standards of care. Finally, fostering a safety climate and culture change creates an environment that prioritizes surgical safety and accountability at both institutional and individual levels. The WHO multimodal strategy, inspired by the successful hand hygiene improvement model, has proven effective in reducing HAIs and is cost-effective. It emphasizes the importance of integrating multiple components to achieve sustainable improvements in IPC practices and SSI prevention. The strategy provides a framework for targeted SSI prevention steps, adaptable to the specific needs and progress levels of healthcare facilities. By applying this model and utilizing supporting resources and tools, a reduction in SSI rates can be achieved.
